title: Aamir Khan Finally Admits What Everyone Already Knew About 'Thugs of Hindostan' — and Why He Can't Even Watch Other People's Films
excerpt: In a remarkably candid interview, the perfectionist opens up about comparing his biggest flop to 'Sholay,' the script changes he couldn't stop, and the screening habit he's too honest to fake.
body:
The man who built a career on meticulous preparation has spent the better part of a decade doing something far harder: admitting he got it spectacularly wrong.

## The Sholay Trap

In a wide-ranging interview that's been making the rounds this week, Aamir Khan finally laid bare the full story behind his decision to join *Thugs of Hindostan* — and the confession is as revealing as it is painful. "The script was like *Sholay*," Khan explained, referring to the 1975 classic that remains Indian cinema's gold standard for ensemble action. "The structure, the way multiple characters come together — it reminded me of *Sholay*. That's what got me."

It's an extraordinary comparison, one that says as much about Khan's ambitions as it does about his blind spots. Where *Sholay* balanced Jai and Veeru's roguish charm with Gabbar Singh's menace across a tight, focused narrative, *Thugs of Hindostan* attempted something far messier — and Khan now knows exactly when it went wrong.

## When the Script Started Changing

The problems began before cameras rolled. Khan revealed that casting changes forced significant script rewrites, shifting the film's focus away from the original ensemble structure that had attracted him in the first place. His character, Firangi — an unreliable, morally slippery con artist — was supposed to sit within a larger tapestry. Instead, the film slowly bent itself around its stars.

"My decision bounced badly," Khan said, with the kind of bluntness that most A-listers reserve for films that flopped at least twenty years ago, not eight.

What makes the admission striking is that Khan reportedly raised concerns about the structural changes *during production*. He saw it happening. He flagged it. And the film barrelled forward anyway. For an actor who famously does only one film at a time, who builds entire years around a single project, that must have stung in ways the box office numbers only partially capture.

## The Screening Confession

But the Thugs revelation wasn't even the week's most telling Khan moment. In what appears to be a separate conversation, Khan also explained why he avoids attending test screenings of other people's films entirely.

"I can't lie," he said. "It'll show on my face."

It's a small admission, but it cuts to the heart of something NRI audiences who grew up on his films understand instinctively: Aamir Khan is constitutionally incapable of performing enthusiasm he doesn't feel. In a Bollywood ecosystem where every premiere is greeted with "masterpiece!" and every star's Instagram story is a festival of mutual adoration, Khan's refusal to play along is both refreshing and slightly terrifying.

## What NRI Fans Hear

For the diaspora, these confessions land differently. If you were one of the thousands of Indian-Americans who booked opening-weekend tickets for *Thugs of Hindostan* in November 2018 — who drove an hour to the nearest theatre showing it, who convinced non-Indian friends that "this is the guy who made *Dangal*" — Khan's honesty reads as belated but earned. The film grossed over ₹300 crore worldwide but left audiences feeling betrayed by the gap between its promise and its delivery.

That Khan is still unpacking it in 2026 suggests the wound runs deeper than commerce. This is a man who genuinely believed he was making the next *Sholay* and watched the ambition curdle in real time.

## What's Next for Khan

Khan's candour comes at an interesting moment. He's been linked to a partition-era biopic about cricketer Lala Amarnath with Ashutosh Gowariker — a reunion with his *Lagaan* director that's generating genuine excitement. Whether that film materialises or not, Khan seems to have entered a phase where protecting his legacy matters less than being honest about it.

In an industry that treats every flop as a "learning experience" and every interview as a branding exercise, there's something quietly radical about a superstar who just says: I saw it was going wrong, I couldn't fix it, and my face can't hide what I think.

*Sources: News Dive, MensXP, Zoom TV Entertainment, Cosmo Planet*
